proof:
# A sharp signed-area theorem for a triangle

Let K be a planar simplex of area k>0, with barycentric coordinates
lambda_0,lambda_1,lambda_2. Define

    C_i={x in K:lambda_i(x)>=1/3},
    D={x in K:at least two C_i contain x}.

Then every compact convex Q subset K satisfies

    |Q|-3|Q intersect D|<=2k/9.                  (1)

The coefficient 2/9 is sharp. This is an ordinary planar auxiliary
theorem, not a mixed-integer depth theorem.

## 1. Normalization and the already proved boundary case

An invertible affine transformation reduces to

    K={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=3}, g=(1,1), |K|=9/2.

Its constant area Jacobian multiplies every term of (1), so proving
the upper bound one in these coordinates proves (1) as stated.
Write E_i for the exclusive portion of cap C_i, and D_ij for the
intersection of caps C_i,C_j. Boundaries have area zero. The E_i are
three parallelograms of area one, and the D_ij are three triangles of
area 1/2, meeting only at g. Let

    J(A)=|A|-3|A intersect D|.

The complete proof in `candidate 4ded4943ded696b8` gives

    J(Q)<=1 whenever g is not interior to Q.      (2)

Its dependencies are explicitly proved there: a supporting/separating
line through g excludes one exclusive cell; cutting away that cell's
complementary trapezoid removes negative area only; horizontal interval
compression then reduces to an exact concave-width integral inequality.
That inequality includes arbitrary projection intervals, boundary values,
and missing square area. In particular (2) includes g on the boundary
without approximation. No unproved localization result is invoked.

It remains to prove the interior case. The following new geometric lemma
supplies that step independently of the unused three-chord reduction.

## 2. A shortest-ray cap has strictly negative signed area

Suppose g belongs to the interior of Q. On the three rays from g through
the vertices of K, let the radial endpoints of Q be g+t_i(v_i-g), where
t_i>0. They exist by compactness; positivity follows from interiority.
Choose an index i minimizing t_i, and put c=t_i>0.

Use affine coordinates (u,v) about g in which its exclusive cone is
u>=0,v>=0 and the three vertex-ray directions are

    (1,1), (-2,1), (1,-2).

For i=0 these coordinates are simply u=1-x,v=1-y; the other choices
are obtained by permuting barycentric coordinates. These permutations
preserve the area of K, so the absolute area Jacobian in the normalized
coordinates is one. The minimality of c and convexity imply that

    q=(c,c), B=(-2c,c), C=(c,-2c)

all belong to Q. Indeed the latter two points are on segments from g
to their respective radial endpoints. The point q is on the boundary
of Q. A supporting line there gives

    Q subset {a u+b v<=c(a+b)}

with (a,b) nonzero. Evaluating this inequality at B and C shows a>=0
and b>=0. It follows that Q has no point with both u>c and v>c.

Let E be Q's area in the positive quadrant, and let D_adj be its area
in the two adjacent double cones:

    u+v>=0, u v<=0.

The triangle conv{q,B,C} is contained in Q. It contains the square
[0,c]^2 and the two triangles

    0<=u<=c, -u<=v<=0,
    0<=v<=c, -v<=u<=0,

whose total area is c^2. These are base portions of the two adjacent
double cones.

By the supporting inequality, the rest of the positive quadrant portion
of Q consists of two disjoint wings, apart from null boundaries:

    W_h=Q intersect {u>=c,0<=v<=c},
    W_v=Q intersect {v>=c,0<=u<=c}.

The square is already in Q, so their areas, counting only their parts
outside the square, satisfy E=c^2+|W_h|+|W_v|. In this formula and below,
the wing intersection along u=c or v=c is a null set.

For the horizontal wing define

    M=max{(u-c)/(v+2c):(u,v) in W_h}.

The maximum is attained because W_h is compact and the denominator is
at least 2c>0. The vertical line segment u=c, -2c<=v<=c belongs to Q.
For 0<=v<=c the horizontal wing section therefore starts at u=c, and
its width is at most M(v+2c). Consequently

    |W_h|<=M integral_0^c(v+2c)dv=(5/2)Mc^2.     (3)

Join a maximizing point to C=(c,-2c). For every -c<=v<=0, this segment
has the point u-c=M(v+2c). Joining that point to the vertical baseline
u=c shows that Q contains

    R_h={-c<=v<=0, 0<=u-c<=M(v+2c)}.

Every point of R_h belongs to the adjacent double cone: u>=c and
v>=-c imply u+v>=0. Its area is

    |R_h|=M integral_-c^0(v+2c)dv=(3/2)Mc^2
          >=(3/5)|W_h|.                         (4)

It is disjoint, up to null boundaries, from the base double triangles,
which have u<=c. The symmetric construction using B provides another
region R_v in the other double cone of area at least (3/5)|W_v|. It is
also disjoint from the base triangles and from R_h, since the two wing
regions have opposite signs of their coordinates. Thus

    D_adj>=c^2+(3/5)(|W_h|+|W_v|)
          =(3/5)E+(2/5)c^2.                      (5)

All statements remain valid if a wing has zero area; then M=0 can be
used and its contribution is zero. No division by a wing area occurs.

The cap C_i has trace u+v>=0. Its exclusive part is precisely E and
its double-covered part is precisely D_adj. Therefore (5) gives

    J(Q intersect C_i)=E-2D_adj
      <=-c^2-(1/5)(|W_h|+|W_v|)<0.               (6)

This proves the required signed-cap assertion with an explicit strict
margin. It does not use the false product bound on the six cone areas.

## 3. Completion of the signed-area theorem

Take i from (6), and let Q_minus be the intersection of Q with the
opposite closed halfplane u+v<=0. This is a compact convex subset of K
with g on its boundary. Equation (2) gives J(Q_minus)<=1. The overlap
of these two pieces is contained in a line and has area zero, including
its intersection with D. Additivity therefore yields

    J(Q)=J(Q intersect C_i)+J(Q_minus)<1.

Together with (2), this proves (1) for every compact convex Q. Empty
and lower-dimensional Q have J(Q)=0 and are also included.

## 4. Sharpness

Take Q=E_i, including its boundary. It is a convex parallelogram of
area 2k/9 and meets D only on null boundaries. Thus J(Q)=2k/9.
Alternatively take the trapezoid formed by two exclusive cells and the
double triangle between them. Its area is 5k/9 and its overlap with D
has area k/9, again giving J(Q)=2k/9.

The strict inequality proved in the interior case also shows that any
equality body of positive area must have g outside its interior. No
classification of all equality cases is asserted.

## Proof dependencies and verification

The full nonstandard concave-width proof is in
`candidate 4ded4943ded696b8`; the attained capacity lemma
used in the separate mixed-fiber application is in
`candidate fbf10959836f7b72`. The present theorem needs only
the former. Both ordinary area additivity and invertible affine changes
have been tracked explicitly. The new wing constants are exactly 5/2,
3/2, and 3/5; no numerical evidence is used.
